grow/exp: Growth that never stops is e to the x: it climbs faster and faster, without end.
grow/room: A real population cannot keep that up: it runs out of land and food.
grow/verhulst: In 1838, the Belgian mathematician Pierre François Verhulst put that in an equation: the bigger a population gets, the more its own size holds its growth back.
grow/S: His curve starts like e to the x, then bends and levels off below a limit it never quite reaches. With the limit at one and the bend at zero, it is this S.
grow/name: That shape gives it its name: sigmoid means shaped like a sigma, the Greek letter S. Its symbol is a small sigma, written like this.
grow/def: In its simplest form, his curve is one over, one plus e to the minus x.
grow/squash: Any number can go in, and what comes out lies between zero and one: near zero far to the left, near one far to the right.
grow/zero: At zero, e to the zero is one, so sigma is one over two: a half, the middle of the S.
grow/two: At two, e to the minus two is small, about zero point one four, so sigma is close to one: about zero point eight eight.
grow/neg: At minus two, e to the minus x is e squared, about seven point three nine. That is big, so sigma is small: about zero point one two.
slope/need: In a graph, a sigmoid node sends the gradient back like any node: times its local slope. So how steep is the S?
slope/n0: Measure it with a nudge. Move x from zero to zero point zero one, and sigma rises by zero point zero zero two five: a slope of a quarter.
slope/slide: Slide along the S, and the tangent tilts less and less. By two, it is much flatter.
slope/n2: There, the same nudge raises sigma by only about zero point zero zero one zero five: a slope of about zero point one zero five.
slope/rule: Verhulst's equation predicts both. In its simplest form, it says the growth rate is how much there is, times how much room is left.
slope/p0: At zero, half the room is filled and half is left: a half times a half is a quarter, the slope we measured.
slope/p2: At two, sigma is about zero point eight eight one, with zero point one one nine left. Their product is about zero point one zero five, again.
slope/formula: So the slope, d sigma, d x, is sigma times one minus sigma, at every x. The node can build it from its own output.
node/plot: Plot that slope at every x, and you get a hill: a quarter at zero, its peak, falling away on both sides.
node/chain: Now a sigmoid node at x equals two, and say a gradient of two arrives from above: partial f, partial sigma.
node/dx: The node multiplies it by its local slope, zero point one zero five, so x gets about zero point two one.
node/most: Wherever x is, the slope is at most a quarter. So x gets at most a quarter of what arrives: with two from above, never more than a half.
flat/six: Far from zero, the S goes flat. At six, sigma is zero point nine nine seven five: the room is all but full.
flat/tiny: With almost no room left, the slope is tiny: about zero point zero zero two five.
flat/mirror: At minus six, the mirror image: almost nothing there yet, so the same tiny slope.
flat/name: A sigmoid stuck near zero or one is called saturated, like a soaked sponge that takes in no more: nudge x, and its output barely moves.
flat/dead: So almost no gradient gets through: with one arriving from above, x gets about zero point zero zero two five.
